title: Boston Man Wins $1 Million Lottery Prize, Then ICE Arrests Him
excerpt: Ariel Velasquez-Morales claimed a $1 million Massachusetts Lottery prize on November 18. Six days later ICE arrested him in East Boston under a removal order issued in 2014.
body:
• Ariel Velasquez-Morales, a Salvadoran national living in East Boston, won $1 million on a $10 Massachusetts Lottery scratch ticket and claimed the prize on November 18.
  • ICE arrested him in East Boston on November 24; the agency says a judge ordered him removed in April 2014 and that he remained in the United States anyway.
  • He chose the cash option on the prize — a one-time payment of $650,000 before taxes — and what happens to the winnings is not yet clear.
  • For readers: a final removal order does not expire. ICE can arrest a person under one at any time, and the agency declined to say whether the lottery's publicity led officers to him.

Last week, the Massachusetts State Lottery was celebrating its newest millionaire: Ariel Velasquez-Morales of East Boston, photographed smiling as he held an oversized check for $1 million. On Tuesday, November 24, officers from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested him in the same neighborhood where he bought the winning ticket, according to an ICE news release announcing the arrest.

Velasquez-Morales won the prize playing the lottery's "$2,000,000 50X Cashword" game, a $10 scratch ticket styled like a crossword puzzle. According to the lottery, it was the first puzzle he had scratched, and he matched 11 words. He claimed the prize on November 18 and chose the cash option, a one-time lump sum of $650,000 before taxes, ICE said. The lottery shared his winner's photograph on social media on November 21; ICE's Boston office later reposted the same image alongside its announcement of the arrest.

"Looks like his luck ran out."

— Micah Bock, ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs

Why ICE says he was arrested

ICE says Velasquez-Morales, a national of El Salvador, entered the United States illegally in 2013 in Texas's Rio Grande Valley, where Border Patrol agents issued him a notice to appear before an immigration judge and released him with a list of free legal service providers. A Department of Justice immigration judge ordered him removed in April 2014, but he remained in the country, the agency said. Three ICE sources told Fox News that he ran briefly when officers moved in on Tuesday morning before being caught, an encounter the sources said was captured on officers' body cameras.

He will remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the United States, according to the release. ICE declined to answer questions from CNN about what led to the arrest or where he is being detained, and CNN reported it could not determine whether he has legal representation. USA Today reported that as of Tuesday evening his name did not appear in ICE's online detainee locator database.

Nothing in lottery law barred the ticket

The win itself broke no lottery rule. Massachusetts bars ticket sales to anyone under 18, and its lottery law says nothing about a player's citizenship or immigration status, as Fox News noted in its reporting. What happens to the $650,000 cash payment now that its winner is in federal custody facing removal is not clear, CNN reported.

The wider enforcement picture

The arrest is one case inside a much larger interior-enforcement campaign. CNN reported that by July 2026 nearly 66,000 people were held in ICE custody, an increase of nearly 70% from the total detained when President Donald Trump took office the year before, with arrests shifting away from the border and into the country's interior. For the diaspora reader, the case is a blunt reminder of how a final removal order works: it carries no expiry date, it can be executed years after it is issued, and a moment of public visibility — even a celebratory one — offers no protection from it.
